projects.title: Laser sensor for CO₂ and H₂O in hydrogen combustion engines
projects.short: A real-time laser absorption sensor that reads temperature and gas composition inside hydrogen engines.
projects.place: Precision Laser Diagnostics Lab · CU Boulder
projects.role: Ph.D. project: I develop the software and hardware of the sensor, including real-time data acquisition and embedded processing.
summary: Hydrogen engines can cut carbon emissions from heavy transport, but controlling their combustion needs fast, in-situ measurements of what is happening inside the engine.

I am developing a laser absorption spectroscopy sensor for CO₂ and H₂O that measures gas temperature and composition directly from the light the molecules absorb, in real time and on the engine itself.

projects.title: Dual-comb spectroscopy and high-temperature spectroscopic databases
projects.short: Broadband, high-resolution measurements to build accurate absorption data for hot H₂O and CO₂.
projects.place: Precision Laser Diagnostics Lab · CU Boulder
summary: Laser sensors are only as accurate as the spectroscopic data used to interpret them. At combustion temperatures, existing databases for H₂O and CO₂ still carry significant uncertainty.
The next stage of my Ph.D. uses dual-comb spectroscopy, which measures thousands of spectral elements at once with high resolution, to help build accurate high-temperature absorption databases.

projects.title: Compact, real-time EGR rate sensor for natural gas engines
projects.short: A shoebox-sized laser sensor that measures exhaust gas recirculation at 954 Hz on a running 250 kW engine.
projects.place: Precision Laser Diagnostics Lab · CU Boulder
summary: Natural gas engines emit about 25 % less greenhouse gas than diesel, but matching diesel efficiency while keeping emissions low requires precise control of the exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) rate.

We built a compact laser absorption sensor based on scanned-wavelength modulation spectroscopy of H₂O. A new, computationally efficient fitting algorithm, Integral Hashing, lets it run autonomously in real time at 954 Hz. The full system, including lasers, drivers, acquisition and processing, fits in a 25 × 25 × 8 cm box powered by 15 W.
On a 250 kW six-cylinder natural gas engine, the sensor agreed with an extractive NDIR analyzer to within 2 % EGR over 0–25 % EGR, and resolved fast transient fluctuations the NDIR could not see.

projects.title: High-speed thermal imaging of disk-shaped firebrands
projects.short: Tracking burning embers at 960 fps to measure how their temperature oscillates as they fly.
projects.place: Precision Laser Diagnostics Lab · CU Boulder
summary: Firebrands (embers) carried by wind can spread wildland fires and ignite structures far from the fire front. Models of their transport need data on how they burn while airborne.

Wooden disks 1.12 mm in diameter were ignited in a new firebrand generator and dropped into a wind tunnel crossflow at 0.4, 1.1 and 2.0 m/s. High-speed colour video at 960 frames per second, combined with particle tracking and two-colour pyrometry, gave the position, velocity and colour temperature of each firebrand over time.

The firebrand temperatures oscillate at distinct frequencies between 50 and 480 Hz, and the frequency correlates with the firebrand's speed relative to the wind, suggesting that fast dynamics matter for firebrand transport models.

projects.title: Solar desalination with phase change materials
projects.short: A passive solar still with coconut oil or paraffin storage, built, tested and modelled in Santiago, Chile.
projects.role: Research assistant: I built and modelled the desalination process.
summary: Fresh-water demand is rising with population growth and climate-driven drought, while most desalination runs on non-renewable energy.

We built and tested a 0.55 m² passive solar desalinator that stores heat in 4.5 kg of coconut oil or paraffin wax inside copper tubes, for three saline-water loads. Annual production ranged from 1120 to 1313 L/m², with coconut oil giving slightly higher productivity per unit of solar energy.
A MATLAB model including the PCM and self-shading predicted condensate mass and phase temperatures with mean RMSE of 0.03 kg and 1.9 °C, at low computational cost.

projects.title: Solar sawdust drying in spouted beds with PCM storage
projects.short: Three spouted beds in series, heated by a solar accumulator holding 89 kg of paraffin wax.
projects.place: University of Santiago of Chile (USACH) · FONDECYT
projects.role: M.Sc. thesis (FONDECYT project): experiments and modelling.
summary: Spouted beds give excellent gas-particle contact for drying, and rectangular-base units connected in series are easier to scale up. We paired them with a solar energy accumulator so drying can continue after sunset.

Experiments: 89 kg of paraffin wax in 450 beverage cans stored solar heat that warmed the drying air for three spouted beds in series. At the optimal conditions the dryer removed 27.6 % of the sawdust moisture, and stored energy could sustain operation for at least 4 hours.

Modelling: energy balances for the accumulator and residence-time distribution, drying kinetics and micro-mixing models for the dryer predicted outlet air temperature within 1.9 °C RMSE and outlet moisture within 5.6 %.
